planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings in spring and plant into well-drained, lean soil; this wild deciduous fig ranges from the Arabian Peninsula and East Africa through the Middle East into the northwestern Himalaya, and is grown chiefly by fig collectors and breeders for its cold- and drought-tolerant genetics rather than for orchard-quality fruit.

directions: Wild Himalayan fig grows as a multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree across arid and semi-arid hill country from Arabia to Pakistan, tolerating rocky, alkaline soils and extended dry spells far better than cultivated Ficus carica. Its small, rough-skinned figs ripen reddish-purple and are palatable but seedy, used locally fresh or dried, and the species is prized mainly by fig breeders seeking cold hardiness, drought tolerance, and resistance genes for crossing into edible fig lines. Grow it in full sun on lean, fast-draining soil and expect strong suckering regrowth after hard freezes or pruning. Because populations vary widely in fruit quality, growers typically propagate from cuttings of selected wild accessions rather than from seed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, gravelly soil; this wild fig from the mountains of Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan dies back to the root in severe winters and resprouts, and is grown mainly by fig breeders for cold-hardiness germplasm.

directions: Afghan fig is a shrubby, extremely cold-tolerant wild relative of the cultivated fig, native to rocky foothills and ravines across the Iranian Plateau and into Afghanistan and Pakistan, where winter temperatures routinely drop well below what Ficus carica can survive. Breeders value it, particularly the afghanistanica forms, as a parent for introducing root and crown hardiness into cultivated fig lines, since plants can be killed to the ground by frost and still regrow and fruit the same season. The small figs are edible but inferior in flavor and size to named carica cultivars, so it is grown almost exclusively for breeding and collecting rather than fresh eating. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and minimal summer water once established, mimicking its native semi-arid mountain habitat.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring into moist, fertile soil; cluster fig is a large tropical Asian tree that fruits directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory), and is grown by tropical fruit collectors and in home gardens across South and Southeast Asia for its edible cooked fruit and cultural significance.

directions: Cluster fig is a fast-growing tropical tree revered across South and Southeast Asia, both for its unusual habit of fruiting in dense clusters directly from the bark of the trunk and main limbs and for its religious importance as one of the sacred fig species. The round, reddish fruits are tough-skinned and gritty-fleshed, generally cooked into curries, pickles, or preserves rather than eaten fresh, though fully ripe fruit can be eaten raw in small quantities. Grow it in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained soil with regular water, as it naturally favors riverbanks and low-lying moist ground in its native range. It needs a frost-free tropical or near-tropical climate and considerable space to reach its full size as a spreading shade and fruiting tree.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil; Himalayan mulberry is a large wild species from mid-elevation Himalayan forests, grown by fruit collectors for its unusually large, long fruit and cold hardiness at altitude.

directions: Himalayan mulberry is a large, long-lived deciduous tree native to mid-elevation forests across the Himalaya from Pakistan to Bhutan, where it is valued locally for fruit that is notably longer and juicier than common white or black mulberry. Trees bear elongated, deep red to nearly black fruit that drops heavily when ripe, and local populations show considerable variation in fruit size and sweetness, making seed-grown and grafted selections of particular interest to mulberry collectors. Grow it in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where it tolerates the cold winters typical of its montane native habitat better than many lowland mulberry species. It needs considerable space to reach its mature size and is generally propagated from hardwood cuttings taken from selected fruiting trees.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in fall or early spring into average, well-drained soil; Mongolian mulberry is a cold-hardy wild species from northern China, Mongolia, Korea, and the Russian Far East, grown by collectors and cold-climate breeders for its hardiness and ornamental deeply lobed leaves.

directions: Mongolian mulberry is a small, exceptionally cold-hardy tree or large shrub native to forests and scrub across northern China, Mongolia, Korea, and the Russian Far East, where winter lows far exceed what common white or black mulberry can tolerate. Its deeply lobed, almost maple-like leaves give it strong ornamental value distinct from other mulberry species, and the small sweet-tart fruit, while less showy than named cultivars, is readily eaten fresh or used in preserves. Grow it in full sun on any well-drained soil; it is adaptable to poor and dry sites and is used by northern breeders as a hardiness parent in cold-climate mulberry improvement work. Its compact size relative to other Morus species also suits smaller gardens and collector plantings.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or container trees in spring into average, well-drained soil; paper mulberry is a fast-growing East Asian Moraceae tree, closely related to the true mulberries, grown by collectors for its curious orange aggregate fruit and historically prized for bark fiber used in papermaking and tapa cloth.

directions: Paper mulberry is a fast-growing, dioecious tree native to East Asia and long cultivated and naturalized across the Pacific and beyond, historically prized for its fibrous inner bark, which is still processed into traditional paper (washi, hanji) and, in the Pacific, beaten into tapa cloth. Female trees produce round, spiky orange aggregate fruit that ripens sweet and is eaten fresh or by birds, though the plant is grown far more for its fiber, shade, and curiosity value among Moraceae collectors than for fruit production. Grow it in full sun on average, well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, disturbed sites, salt spray, and urban pollution, and spreads readily by root suckers in favorable climates. Because of its vigorous suckering and seed dispersal by birds, it should be sited and managed carefully in warmer zones where it can become locally weedy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring into fertile, well-drained tropical soil; dyer's mulberry is a tropical American relative of Osage orange grown by Moraceae and tropical fruit collectors for its small edible mulberry-like fruit and historic use as a yellow dyewood (old fustic).

directions: Dyer's mulberry, also called old fustic, is a large tropical American tree ranging from Mexico and the Caribbean south to Argentina, closely related to Osage orange and bearing small, sweet, mulberry-like aggregate fruit relished by birds and occasionally eaten by people. Its dense yellow heartwood was historically a major source of fustic dye, used for centuries to produce yellow and olive-green textile colors before synthetic dyes became common, and the wood remains valued for durability. Grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a frost-free tropical or subtropical climate, where it develops into a substantial shade tree with a broad, rounded crown. It is grown today mainly by tropical fruit and Moraceae collectors and in agroforestry plantings rather than as a conventional orchard crop.
